Why Correlation Matters

If two things you own always move together, owning both does not spread your risk. Correlation tells you which markets move together, which move opposite, and which are unrelated, so you can see how diversified you really are.

Links change with the times. In calm markets Bitcoin can move on its own; in a panic it often falls together with tech stocks. Gold tends to rise when the US dollar weakens. Always look at the rolling chart, not just one number.

Questions & Answers

What does correlation mean?

Correlation measures how two markets move day to day, from −1 to +1. Near +1 they rise and fall together; near −1 one tends to rise when the other falls; near 0 there is no reliable link.

Is Bitcoin correlated with the Nasdaq?

Often, yes. Since 2020 Bitcoin has frequently moved with tech stocks, especially in sell-offs, but the link comes and goes. The rolling chart above shows how strong it is right now.

Is gold a hedge against stocks or crypto?

Gold usually has a low or slightly negative link to stocks and crypto, which is why investors use it to diversify. It often moves opposite to the US dollar.

Where does the stock market data come from?

Daily closing levels of the S&P 500, the Nasdaq Composite and the Dow Jones, and the 10-year US Treasury yield, come from the US Federal Reserve's FRED database. We show only % performance and correlations, not the index levels themselves.

What does the 10-year yield tell me?

It is the interest rate on 10-year US government bonds. When it rises quickly, it often weighs on gold, tech stocks and crypto, because safe bonds pay more. A negative correlation with these assets shows that pull.

Does correlation predict prices?

No. It describes how markets have moved together in the past. Relationships change, sometimes suddenly. Use it as context, not as a signal to buy or sell.
